questions.q: The noiseless shot run gave `{'00': 503, '11': 521}` against an exact 50/50 ideal split. Why is this deviation attributed to sampling noise rather than hardware error?
options: Because 1024 shots is too few to mean anything
Because no noise model was attached to this run, so there is no hardware-error mechanism available to explain it -- only finite-shot sampling variation remains as an explanation
Because 00 and 11 are impossible outcomes
Because the statevector result also showed a 503/521 split
questions.explain: With zero noise model attached, the only possible source of deviation from the exact 0.5/0.5 split is statistical sampling noise from a finite number of shots.

questions.q: The noisy shot run produced small but nonzero `01` and `10` counts (11 and 8). Why can these specifically NOT be explained by sampling noise alone?
options: Because sampling noise only affects the `00` outcome
Because the exact ideal circuit gives P(01)=P(10)=0 exactly, so no amount of noiseless sampling, however large, would ever be expected to produce a nonzero count there
Because 4096 shots is always enough to eliminate sampling noise
Because `01` and `10` were also seen in the noiseless run
questions.explain: Sampling noise can only vary the split among outcomes that are already possible. Since the ideal circuit makes `01`/`10` exactly impossible, any nonzero count there must come from an actual error mechanism, not finite-sample variation.

questions.q: In the noisy run, the `00` and `11` counts (2090 and 1987) differ from both the noiseless 2048/2048 expectation and the noisy exact 2038/2038 expectation. What explains this combined pattern?
options: A bug in the simulator
Two stacked sources of deviation: the real noise-driven shift in the 00/11 split, plus ordinary sampling noise layered on top
Only sampling noise -- noise models never affect the 00/11 split
Only gate noise -- sampling noise doesn't apply once a noise model is present
questions.explain: A real noisy result reflects both the actual noise-driven shift away from the ideal split AND the usual shot-to-shot sampling variation on top of it -- both effects are present simultaneously.

questions.q: What is the general diagnostic rule for judging whether an observed count in real results indicates genuine hardware error?
options: Any deviation from a perfect even split always indicates hardware error

Check whether a noiseless simulation of the same circuit at the same shot count could plausibly produce the same deviation through sampling noise alone; if the outcome is one the ideal circuit rules out entirely, any nonzero count is a real signal
Hardware error can only be detected by running more shots
Noiseless simulation is irrelevant to interpreting real hardware results
questions.explain: The core diagnostic habit: deviations among already-possible outcomes are usually just sampling noise (quantifiable via the standard-error formula), while any nonzero count on an outcome the ideal circuit rules out entirely cannot be explained by sampling noise and signals real error.

questions.q: Which of the three runs in this lab provides the only result with exactly zero uncertainty?
options: The noiseless shots run (b)
The noisy shots run (c)
The noiseless statevector run (a)
None of them have zero uncertainty
questions.explain: Statevector simulation (run a) computes exact amplitudes directly with no sampling involved at all, making it the only one of the three with zero statistical uncertainty -- true ground truth rather than an estimate.
